about.title: About our practice
about.text:
At The GI Guy, we are dedicated to expert gastroenterology care with a compassionate, holistic approach. Led by Dr. Kurt Vernon, our practice has served the Greater Raleigh area for over 20 years from two offices in Fuquay-Varina and Dunn, NC.

We use the most advanced technology available, including FUSE™ endoscopy, which gives some of the highest available detection rates for colon cancer, and we create a unique atmosphere where patients come first.

Our approach looks at your health as a whole: we provide education, incorporate nutrition and lifestyle, and recommend only the best quality products.

doctor.name: Kurt Vernon, MD, FACG
doctor.quote: The secret to successful treatment is personalized care. I always take the time to work one-on-one with patients during their program. My patients know that I am always available for them. I explain everything I do and encourage patients to ask questions. In the end, they aren't just healed, they're educated, too.
doctor.bio:
Kurt Vernon, MD is a board-certified gastroenterologist and a Fellow of the American College of Gastroenterology, the American College of Physicians and the American Anti-Aging Academy, with over 20 years of experience.

Dr. Vernon has the expertise and advanced technology to accurately diagnose and treat a wide range of colon, liver, digestive and rectal conditions, including cancer screening, abdominal pain, ulcers, irritable bowel syndrome and heartburn/reflux. Add in his bedside manner and caring personality, and it's easy to see why over 90% of his patients come from referrals. Many of our patients are physicians and medical professionals themselves.

Dr. Vernon is board-certified in internal medicine and gastroenterology by the American Board of Internal Medicine, and he continually works to refine his skills and use the latest medical techniques.

faqs.q: What is a colonoscopy, and why is it important?
faqs.a: A colonoscopy examines the inside of your colon for polyps, abnormalities or signs of colon cancer. It is the only test that can both detect and prevent colon cancer, because polyps can be removed during the procedure.

In a study of 10,000 average-risk people, Cologuard found 92% of colon cancers. It is non-invasive and needs no prep, but it does not reliably find precancerous polyps, and a positive result needs a follow-up colonoscopy. [Read more about Cologuard](article.html?id=cologuard).

faqs.q: What should I expect during a flexible sigmoidoscopy?
faqs.a: It is a quick, minimally invasive screening of the lower colon. It typically takes less than 30 minutes and needs minimal preparation.
Endoscopy is very safe when performed by experienced specialists. Risks are small; some patients have minor discomfort afterward. Our team looks after your safety throughout.

faqs.q: How do I prepare for my procedure?
faqs.a: It depends on the procedure. A colonoscopy requires a clear-liquid diet and bowel prep. We'll give you instructions for your procedure, and you can download the [colonoscopy prep instructions](patients.html#prep) here.
We accept Medicare, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Cigna, Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, Wellpath and many others. Please call (919) 577-0085 to confirm your coverage.

organs.name: Stomach
organs.text: A J-shaped organ just left of center, between the esophagus and the small intestine. Protein digestion begins here.

organs.name: Small intestine
organs.text: Folded into much of the abdomen, it does most of the digestion and absorption of nutrients. Enzymes and bile break food into small building blocks that pass into the bloodstream. The duodenum is its first, C-shaped section.

organs.name: Colon
organs.text: The large intestine wraps around the small intestine like a frame. It absorbs water from what's left of digested food and moves waste out of the body.

organs.name: Rectum
organs.text: The last 6–8 inches of the large intestine. It holds stool until it leaves the body.

organs.name: Liver
organs.text: The largest internal organ. It stores vitamins, sugars and fats and releases them as needed; builds the proteins that clot blood and make new cells; filters waste from the blood; and breaks down harmful substances like alcohol.

organs.name: Gallbladder
organs.text: A small organ under the liver on the right side. It stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the intestine to help digest fats.

organs.name: Pancreas
organs.text: A fish-shaped organ behind the stomach. It makes hormones like insulin and glucagon, and digestive enzymes that it sends to the small intestine.

quiz.title: Are you at risk for colon cancer?
quiz.intro: Gastrointestinal problems account for more hospitalizations in the U.S. than any other group of disorders. Answer these quick questions to see whether you should talk with us about screening. Your answers stay on your device.
questions: Have you had colon polyps or colon cancer before?
Has a parent, sibling or child had colon polyps or colon cancer?
Have you had diarrhea or constipation for more than 3 weeks?
Do you have a family history of pancreatic, breast or uterine cancer?
Have you seen any blood in or on your stool?
Have you had unexplained weight loss?
Do you have familial polyposis syndrome?
Do you have unexplained abdominal pain?
quiz.yesResult: Based on your answers, you may benefit from colon cancer screening or an evaluation. Please call us to schedule a visit with Dr. Vernon.
quiz.noResult: You answered no to every question. Keep up with routine checkups, and call us if anything changes. Any screening is better than none.

articles.title: Cologuard technology
articles.summary: A no-prep, no-sedation screening option for colon cancer, and how it compares to colonoscopy.
articles.body:
Testing for colon cancer just got easier. Cologuard is a colon cancer screening test that is simple to use. It involves no prep, no sedation, and most importantly, it's effective.

## What exactly is Cologuard?
Cologuard tests for genetic changes in stool that are associated with colon cancer. It correctly identifies 92% of people who have colon cancer. It will not, however, lower your risk of developing cancer, because it cannot reliably detect precancerous polyps. If a Cologuard test comes back positive, a follow-up colonoscopy will be recommended.

## How does it work?
DNA is continuously shed from cells in the intestinal lining into stool. If cancer or precancer is present, abnormal cells are shed along with normal ones. Cologuard looks for altered DNA and/or blood in the stool that may signal cancer or precancer.

## How effective is it?
In a study of 10,000 people at average risk for colon cancer, Cologuard found 92% of cancers. It was negative in 87% of people without the disease.

## Should colonoscopy be used as well?
Cologuard is a screening test. Any positive result should be discussed with your doctor and followed by a diagnostic colonoscopy.

## The bottom line
Colon cancer is common. Colonoscopy is the only test proven to both detect and prevent colon cancer, because precancerous polyps are removed during the procedure. About one in three patients has polyps removed during a colonoscopy. For people who don't want a colonoscopy, Cologuard is one alternative.

Remember: any colon cancer screening test is better than none. Learn more at [cologuard.com](https://www.cologuard.com/).

articles.title: What is an endoscopy?
articles.summary: How an endoscope lets your doctor see inside your digestive tract, and why it might be recommended.
articles.body:
An endoscopy is a nonsurgical procedure that lets your doctor look inside your digestive tract with a thin camera called an endoscope. In an upper endoscopy, the endoscope passes through the mouth and throat to view the esophagus, stomach and first part of the small intestine. It is usually a quick outpatient procedure.

An endoscope can also view the large intestine (the colon) through the rectum. Your physician may recommend an endoscopy to evaluate:

- Stomach problems or pain
- Bowel pain or diarrhea
- Other digestive tract problems
- Ulcers
- Polyps, growths or other colon findings

Sometimes your physician will take a small tissue sample (a biopsy) during the procedure to check for disease. Ask your doctor to explain as much as possible beforehand so you're prepared.

If you have questions about an endoscopy or a related procedure, please call our office.

articles.title: Dr. Vernon receives BCBSNC Tier 1 recognition
articles.summary: Our practice received a Tier 1 Designation from Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina for high quality and cost efficiency.
articles.body:
The practice of Kurt Vernon, MD, The GI Guy, is proud to announce that we have received a Tier 1 Designation, a high-quality recognition from one of the nation's largest health insurers, [Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina](https://www.bluecrossnc.com/).

The BCBSNC Tiered Network uses claims data to identify high-quality, low-cost providers and help consumers make more informed choices about their care. Our practice was scored on gastroenterology quality measures, including colonoscopy and GERD care.

"It is a pleasure to be recognized by BCBSNC as a Tier 1 North Carolina gastroenterologist. We will continue to improve upon our quality measures to provide the best care for our patients," said Dr. Vernon.

The designation compares physician performance with peers on nationally accepted quality measures and local cost-efficiency benchmarks, within the same region and specialty. Practices that exceed both the quality and cost thresholds are designated Tier 1.

fasttrack.title: Positive Cologuard® or stool test? Get your colonoscopy in 7–14 days.
fasttrack.intro: A positive stool test doesn't mean you have cancer, but the only way to know is a colonoscopy. In many places that means waiting months, and the waiting is the hardest part. With Fast-Track, we usually schedule your colonoscopy within 7–14 days of your phone screening.
fasttrack.noVisit: No office visit needed first. If you're generally healthy, we screen you by phone, send your prep instructions and schedule your procedure.

steps.title: Call us
steps.text: Tell us you had a positive Cologuard®, FIT or other stool test. Have your result, insurance card and medication list handy.

steps.title: Phone screening
steps.text: Our staff asks a short list of health questions. If you're healthy enough for a direct colonoscopy, you skip the separate office visit.

steps.title: Prep instructions
steps.text: We send your bowel prep instructions: exactly what to buy, eat and drink before your procedure.

steps.title: Your colonoscopy
steps.text: Dr. Vernon performs your colonoscopy, usually within 7–14 days, and goes over the results with you.

fasttrack.fit:
You had a positive (abnormal) Cologuard®, FIT or other stool-based colon cancer test
You're generally healthy
You'd rather not wait months to find out
fasttrack.notFit:
Take blood thinners such as warfarin, Eliquis, Xarelto or Plavix
Have serious heart, lung or kidney disease
Have had problems with anesthesia or sedation
Have symptoms like heavy bleeding or severe abdominal pain
fasttrack.notFitNote: That doesn't rule you out. It just means Dr. Vernon reviews your history first. Our staff will tell you on the call.
fasttrack.bring:
Your positive test result (or the name of the doctor who ordered it)
Your insurance card
A list of your medications
A driver for the day of your procedure
fasttrack.insurance: Many insurance plans, including Medicare, now treat a colonoscopy after a positive stool test as part of screening, which can mean little or no out-of-pocket cost. Coverage varies, so our staff will check your plan when you call.

faqs.q: Does a positive stool test mean I have cancer?
faqs.a: No. Most people with a positive stool test do not have cancer. The test can be positive because of polyps, hemorrhoids or other causes. A colonoscopy is the only way to know, and polyps found during it can be removed on the spot.

faqs.q: Why do I need a colonoscopy if I already did a stool test?
faqs.a: A stool test only tells us something may be there. A colonoscopy lets Dr. Vernon see the whole colon and remove polyps before they can turn into cancer.
Some insurance plans require one. If yours does, we can request it from the doctor who ordered your stool test.

faqs.q: I don't live near Fuquay-Varina or Dunn. Can I still come?
faqs.a: Yes. Patients come to us from across North Carolina so they don't have to wait. Most people only make one trip, on the day of the procedure.

faqs.q: How fast can I be seen?
faqs.a: We usually schedule your colonoscopy within 7–14 days of your phone screening, depending on your health history, your insurance and your prep.

fasttrack.providers: If your patient has a positive stool test and is facing a long wait, send them our way. Fax the referral and the stool test result to our Fuquay-Varina office at (919) 577-0013 or our Dunn office at (910) 891-5323, and we'll call your patient to complete the phone screening. We send the colonoscopy and pathology reports back to you.
fasttrack.homeBand: **Positive Cologuard® or stool test?** Get your colonoscopy in 7–14 days. No office visit needed first.
